children: Student loan defaults have been rising this year and the numbers are likely to get worse, recent survey data suggest. Defaults hit a record high this year, just before the roll out of the Trump administration's new federal repayment rules, which have increased costs for many borrowers' monthly payments even higher.

An estimated 67% of borrowers have said they would be unable to afford their new monthly student loan payment following the July changes, a survey by the Student Debt Crisis Center found. The organization surveyed more than 3,200 respondents in the U.S. and found that the new median monthly increase in student loan payments was $500, according to their analysis.

In the next week, the Education Department is expected to release default data for the group of borrowers who entered repayment in 2023 and a rise in the three-year average is expected for the first time since the pandemic era. The latest Federal Reserve Bank of New York data released Aug. 10 shows the student loan delinquency rate in the second quarter increased to 10.6% of balances more than 90 days past due, up from 10.3% reported in the first quarter.

Meanwhile, other survey data suggests borrowers are losing faith in the system. Richard Richtmyer, student loans managing editor at Credible, says that the lending platform is aware of the surge in student loan defaults. "The repayment system changed faster than borrowers could keep up with," he says. "Many people may have lost track of the plan they are on and what they owe."

Candidly, which provides student loan counseling through employers, found last summer that 57% of users didn't know who their student loan servicer was, and 46% didn't know how much they owe. Carli Reddy, Head of Coaching at Candidly says her company saw a 460% increase in workers turning to them for guidance after the change in repayment rules were announced.
"Borrowers who are trying to get back on track are just really having a tough time getting their head above water," says Reddy.
Confusion about the status of the governments' collection efforts is also widespread. In 2025, the government announced it would begin collections, although it has since paused them.

"The federal government started collections again, but they put that on pause," says Richtmyer. But he warns, "borrowers shouldn't read that as a grace period. It's not a policy change and there's no announced end date. They could resume at any time."

What to do. The worst thing borrowers can do, even if they feel they are unable to afford payments, is to just ignore the matter, Richtmyer says. "The single most effective thing a borrower can do now is contact their servicer, before they miss a payment. Once you are in default, your options narrow considerably," he says.

Look for other options beyond federal student loans. Several states, including Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Connecticut, have sought to expand state student loan options to help fill the financing gap.

But federal loans may be the best option. Scott Bishop, a partner and managing director at Houston-based Presidio Wealth Partners, says that "federal loans can come with repayment options and protections that may not be available with a private or state-based loan, including certain income-driven repayment options, deferment or forbearance provisions, and potential forgiveness or discharge programs."

Financial advisors' role. Advisors should run a financial plan for parents of students which takes into consideration how retirement will look should they help their child with education costs or cosign a student loan, Bishop says.

"That analysis may show that helping a child with college means working three or five years longer, spending less today, accepting a lower standard of living in retirement, or taking more investment risk than they otherwise would," he says.
